claims.text: Carbon supersaturation in HEA multilayer coatings stabilizes the coating microstructure.
Carbon supersaturation pins dislocations in HEA multilayer coatings.
Carbon supersaturation locks grain boundaries in HEA multilayer coatings.
Microstructural stabilization caused by carbon supersaturation reduces time-dependent plastic deformation relative to coatings without deliberate carbon supersaturation.
Introducing a carbon-supersaturated layer by controlled magnetron sputtering produces the relevant modified HEA multilayer structure.
Carbon atoms segregate to grain boundaries and defects in the HEA film.
Carbon accumulated at grain boundaries and elsewhere in the microstructure restricts dislocation motion.
Carbon accumulated at grain boundaries restricts grain-boundary sliding.
Dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding are movements underlying time-dependent plastic deformation in these coatings.
Restricting dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding enhances resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Under identical mechanical and thermal conditions, carbon-supersaturated HEA coatings will have a significantly lower time-dependent deformation rate than non-carbon-supersaturated coatings.
Carbon-supersaturated HEA coatings will exhibit reduced creep strain or delayed deformation onset relative to the baseline.
The proposed behavior applies within a composition-dependent carbon-solubility and segregation window under moderate temperature and stress conditions.
Changing alloy composition may change carbon solubility, carbon segregation, and therefore the deformation response.
